questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I really wanted to learn/improve my spanish level, and Uniandes offers a free spanish summer course, along with spanish course during the real semester. Plus colombian spanish is easier than a lot of other dialects. Bogotá also seemed like a really interesting city.
Find a lot of useful info here in the Uniandes student handbook: Student handbook:
https://www.calameo.com/read/0063719329db1bfebcfd5

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I highly highly recommend going to Uniandes, it's really nice for a bunch of reasons:
- Colombians are great and hospitibal people and are easy to make friends with. I knew close to no one who didn't make colombian friends to some degree
- The spanish summer course offers you a chance to create a social circle before starting starting the semester. Everyone there is looking for new friends in a foreign place, so it's very social. 
- Bogotá is located super central, so plenty of fun weekend trips to be had
- Bogotá in itself is really a fun city, there's sooo much culture and it's a melting pot of the country's cultures. Plus the climate is like danish april/may weather all year
- The flights are expensive, but living there can be really cheap if you want it to.
- At uniandes there's a group of local students in charge of integrating the exchange students, meaning there's a lot of events and opportunities to meet other exchange students. 
- Colombia really has a strong beating heart, it's one of those countries you can't help but fall in love with
- People who choose Colombia as an exhange destionation rather than something more conventional are often quite fun and interesting. Plus there's a good age-mix since many also go during their masters. I'm 25 and didn't feel too old. If you want to go to Rosklide and it overlaps with the first days of the summer course you can skip a couple of days (but not something like a week), attendance is registered and mandatory like in gymnasiet. 
Safety wise Bogotá is mared strongly by armed robberies, it happens a lot. I was robbed four times. But everytime it happened close to a park called Parque de los periodistas, so stay away from there and that helps alot. Also, there's a culture of almost only robbing men, i know maybe 20 men (local and foreign) who've been robbed, and only one woman. One the plus side, robbery is more or less the only danger in Bogotá itself, and it really rarely turns violent, so just consider it part of your travel budget. Ask locals how to take precautions. To stay safe in the rest of the country, avoid the guerilla controled areas (see british foreign travel advice and ask locals), and be aware of robberies in all big cities. Besides that it's no worries.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Talked to someone from KU who had been on exhange there earlier. 
Exhange students generally live in two types of places: 
1. CityU and LivinnX (mostly livinnX). These are huge blocks close to Uni with shared apartments. Location is great, and convinent because many people live there. But it's really expensive and quite sterile. I found that people (myself included) were genrally more happy with option 2. 
2. Old houses and random apartments in La Candelaria. I lived in one of these with a huge room and private balcony for 1.3 million COP per month - you can find prices down to 600 k COP. The house was shared with 7 other mostly exhange students + plus the owner and his two older sons. It's really nice. It's called K&J's House Bogotá on facebook. Only downside was that 6 of the others were french girls, so sometimes they just spoke french with each other. Another similar option is Casa del Sol in La Candelaria. It's nice and fun, but again stuffed with french people so you might feel outside at times. 

A few people found housing in chapinero but hated the long daily comute. 

Many people showed up without having found housing before arriving and often found good word of mouth options this way.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
As an exhange student you get first pick for all courses before local students, so you can pretty much get the classes you want. The uni dosn't restrict you to pick courses within your field. You can take up to 20 credits, but only need 12. 

If you see a course that looks interesting (or the language course fx), but find that you have to stressful a schedule, you can often just sign up for it and talk with the professor about allowing you to take the course as an "assistant". Meaning you can attend classes and readings but don't get credits for the course and don't have to do any hand-ins/exams. You can freely drop courses until sometime in October. So pick more courses than you need and drop the ones you like the lease (uniandes recommends this too). 

Notice that course workload varies insanely across courses. So it can be nice to take some creative courses to soften up the workload in case you get unlucky. 
Many professors will allow you to do hand-ins in english rather than spanish, but you have to ask the specific profe about it. Bachelor courses are usually wastly less work heavy than masters courses.

How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Super different. Classes have frequent hand-ins and are way smallers (often 20 ppl or the like). Attendance is mandatory, but how mandatory depends on the professor. Often you can skip up to 15%.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Summer spanish (ELE 2) 
- Semester spanish (ELE 3)
- Ceramicá Basica
Take ceramics!! It's really nice (10 ects) and you only have to pay for clay. 
- Taller de dibujar basica
Really fun drawing course, you don't need any previous drawing experince to do it (same with ceramics)
- Escalar 
Climbing course, okay but the facilies are not that good
- Billar
Fun course, but they play a colombian version of billard and it's very technique oriented but you always play
- ECOPOLÍTICA Y POÉTICA DE LOS PENSAMIENTOS INDÍGENAS LATINOAMERICANOS-PROBLEMAS ANTROPOL. CONTEMP 
Super interesting, but attended it as assistant because the workload is insane.

questions.answer:
I travelled around a lot, so that got somewhat expensive. The semester ends start december, so you can travel for two months before your next semester at KU if you want and can afford it. 

Using Uber daily (kind of) is necessary due to security, but it's really cheap. Motorbike ubers are cheaper and more fun but also kind of dangerous (a lot of crashes). NEVER HAUL A TAXI!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
If you wanna see somewhere that no other people go, Gachalá is really nice for a weekendtrip. Good for hiking, and there's a direct local bus leaving from somewhere in Chapinero. 

Other than that there's a million options, but you'll learn about them when u arrive.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
People are super welcoming, so don't worry about it. 
My spanish was quite basic when i arrived, but locals are happy to talk to you anyway. Most young uni people know english, but will address you in spanish anyway unless you insist or really struggle in spanish.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: People in class will often want to make friends with you, so just be open to it. Creative classes can be great because you have time to hang out it class.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The language, it's tiring but super rewarding. 

Plus there's sometime a toxic vibe amoung young local people that it's looking down on a bit to go home early from a party.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The love and warth of the people, hard to find better anywhere in the world. Plus the cultural diversity of the country is breathtaking. About 70 indiginous language still get spoken.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Do it!!!! I was scared before going too, trust me it's the right decision!!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: For brushing up your spanish (or learning it) before going, i recommend getting a language exchange partner in Copenhagen, it's the best way to improve. You might find one through Studieskolen or the app Hello Talk.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The time during the spanish summer course was really magical.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Improving my spanish.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Do it!!
